Ubisoft cuts 166 jobs at Montreal and Qu: Canada's biggest games employer is shrinking again. 166 jobs are cut, 128 in Montréal and 38 in Québec City, less than 4% of Ubisoft's Canadian staff. Its Halifax studio closed in January and its Winnipeg studio in June.
Movie studios sue Bell for millions over: Film companies say Bell failed to pass piracy notices on to its subscribers, and reports have put the claim in the hundreds of millions of dollars. How courts treat internet providers here could affect any Canadian rights holder. We have not read today's article, so open it to see what changed.

Death to Canada’s film scene?: A short opinion video by Toronto Sun columnist Brian Lilley about a proposed US tax-credit bill, backed by Trump, that he says may ruin film production in Canada. It is one columnist's view, and we have not seen the bill's details. Canada's own credits are explained on our Status & Tax Credits page.
Canada’s film and television industry is: An opinion column by the Globe's film editor, Barry Hertz, on the new federal budget. Its headline says film and TV is being left in the dark. Other Globe stories this week say the budget gives the cultural sector a $4-billion boost and gives CBC/Radio-Canada money. We could not read past the paywall, so open it for the column's reasons.
Skywild Pictures buys Niv Fichman’s Rhom: Rhombus Media, founded by Niv Fichman in 1979 and behind BlackBerry and The Sympathizer, has been bought by Skywild Pictures, which launched in 2025. Rhombus will run as a semi-autonomous label, Fichman stays on as lead producer, and the two companies' scripted slates combine, with Rhombus alone reporting about 25 projects in development. Terms were not disclosed. Producers are post's clients, so who owns the slate matters.

Why Trump Is Throwing His Weight Behind: President Trump is pushing Congress to pass a federal film and TV tax credit. As proposed, per Screen International, it would be a 20% transferable credit that covers wages, post-production and VFX, for productions that spend at least $1 million and shoot at least three-quarters of their days in the US. It is a proposal, not law, and critics tell TIME such incentives do not create lasting jobs. If it passes, it competes directly with Canadian service work, including post and VFX.
Miller, Solomon name AI and culture coun: Ottawa announced in March that it would set up an Advisory Council on AI and Culture, a joint effort of culture minister Marc Miller and AI minister Evan Solomon, to advise on the creative sector as the government shapes AI legislation. Means & Ways reported it would have 12 rotating members. Playback says the members are now named; we have not read that article, so open it for the names.
Telefilm Canada names Erin Burke as nati: Telefilm Canada has named Erin Burke national director of feature film for the English market. Playback reported she had been the interim director since January. This is the person who leads Telefilm's English-language feature work, so it matters to producers, and to the Editors and post houses who work on those films. We have not read the full Cartt article, which is behind a paywall.
Does GenAI Belong At Animation Festivals: Manchester Animation Festival will stop accepting films made with generative AI from 2027. Chris Robinson of the Ottawa International Animation Festival says Ottawa will take its cues from its community rather than ban it, and says some entrants hide AI use on their forms. If you animate or do VFX in Canada, expect festivals to ask you to disclose how AI was used.
‘The Tree’ Director Julie Bertuccelli Te: French director Julie Bertuccelli told an audience at India's film festival that a Canadian producer "stole" her planned adaptation of Henning Mankell's Italian Shoes, which was set to shoot in Canada. She did not name the producer or give the full story, so this is her account only, and we have not seen a response. It matters to Canadian producers and the crews who depend on them because international co-productions run on trust.
Amélie Hoeferle & Graham Campbell Filmin: Fake Skating, a feature with working title Winterlong, is shooting in Winnipeg from November 2 to December 11, 2026, with a release date listed as July 16, 2027. That leaves about seven months from wrap to release, so its post schedule will be tight. We have not seen where the post work will be done.
$9.9M for 12 film and TV projects in nor: Ontario is investing more than $9.9 million through the Northern Ontario Heritage Fund Corporation in 12 film and television projects, which the province says will create about 600 local jobs. The fund says it has put nearly $172 million into 234 northern projects since 2018. The province's release talks about production spending and jobs in the north, and does not say how much of that will be post-production work.
Irish-Canadian spy series Tanner wins tw: Tanner, a six-part Irish-Canadian spy drama from Fíbín Films and Toronto's Rhombus Media, won two awards at the TV Beats market in Tallinn on November 18: a presentation slot at Gothenburg's TV Drama Vision in January 2027 and a place as a Conecta 2027 finalist. It is still in development, so there is no post work yet. It shows Canadian companies partnering on European series, which can bring Canadian post work later.
